kashk.name: Kashk
kashk.summary: A dried dairy product made from strained yogurt or buttermilk, popular across Iranian, Caucasian and Central Asian cuisines, known variously as kashk, qurut or keshk.

shahnameh.name: Shahnameh
shahnameh.summary: An epic poem of about 50,000 couplets written by the Persian poet Ferdowsi between around 977 and 1010 CE, telling Iran's mythical and historical past up to the Muslim conquest. It is regarded as Iran's national epic.

ferdowsi.name: Ferdowsi
ferdowsi.summary: Persian poet (940–1025) who wrote the Shahnameh, one of the world's longest epic poems by a single author and one of the greatest works in Persian literature.

middle-persian.name: Middle Persian
middle-persian.summary: A Western Iranian language that became the literary language of the Sasanian Empire and is the linguistic ancestor of modern Persian.

jameh-mosque-of-nain.name: Jameh Mosque of Nain
jameh-mosque-of-nain.summary: A Shi'ite Friday mosque in Nain, Iran, one of the country's oldest, added to Iran's National Heritage List in 1932.

jameh-mosque-of-isfahan.name: Jameh Mosque of Isfahan
jameh-mosque-of-isfahan.summary: A historic congregational mosque in Isfahan, Iran, built and reworked from around 771 CE onward, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012.

arthur-upham-pope.name: Arthur Upham Pope
arthur-upham-pope.summary: American scholar and art historian, an expert on Persian art who edited the Survey of Persian Art (1939).

hadith.name: Hadith
hadith.summary: Islamic oral traditions reporting the words, actions and approvals of the prophet Muhammad or his companions, compiled and graded for authenticity from the 7th to 10th centuries.

pendentive.name: Pendentive
pendentive.summary: A triangular architectural device letting a circular or elliptical dome sit over a square or rectangular room, first tried by the Romans and fully developed in Constantinople's Hagia Sophia.

squinch.name: Squinch
squinch.summary: An architectural element that supports a round or octagonal dome on a square base, originating in Sassanid Persia and later used in Islamic, Georgian and Armenian buildings.

taq-e-bostan.name: Taq-e Bostan
taq-e-bostan.summary: A site of large Sasanian rock reliefs near Kermanshah, Iran, carved around the 4th century CE, among the finest examples of Sassanid Persian sculpture.

khosrow-ii.name: Khosrow II
khosrow-ii.summary: Last great pre-Islamic monarch of Iran, ruling the Sasanian Empire from 590 to 628; he conquered Roman territory in the Middle East before being deposed and killed by his own son.

nishapur.name: Nishapur
nishapur.summary: A city in northeastern Iran, founded in the 3rd century by Shapur I, later capital of the Tahirid dynasty and initial capital of the Seljuk Empire.

hisham-s-palace.name: Khirbat al-Mafjar
hisham-s-palace.summary: An early Islamic archaeological site near Jericho built by the Umayyad dynasty in the 8th century, with a palace, bath complex and one of the world's largest continuous mosaic floors.

maurice-emperor.name: Maurice
maurice-emperor.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 582 to 602 and the last of the Justinian dynasty, a successful general who ended the war with Persia and campaigned extensively against the Avars in the Balkans; he lived 539–602.

phocas.name: Phocas
phocas.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 602 to 610 who rose from the army to overthrow Emperor Maurice, and was himself overthrown and executed by Heraclius.

heraclius.name: Heraclius
heraclius.summary: Byzantine emperor from 610 to 641 who seized power in a revolt against Phocas, then fought long wars against Persia and the Arabs, driving the Persians from Asia Minor before losing territory to Arab conquests.

battle-of-al-qadisiyyah.name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
battle-of-al-qadisiyyah.summary: A battle fought in November 636 in which the Rashidun Caliphate decisively defeated the Sasanian Empire, opening the way to the Persian capital of Ctesiphon and the eventual conquest of Persia.

umar.name: Umar
umar.summary: Second Rashidun caliph, ruling 634 to 644; a close companion of Muhammad whose conquests brought Persia and much of the Byzantine Empire under Muslim rule before his assassination.

battle-of-nineveh-627.name: Battle of Nineveh (627)
battle-of-nineveh-627.summary: The climactic 627 battle of the Byzantine-Sasanian War, in which Emperor Heraclius's forces defeated and killed the Persian commander Rhahzadh, later triggering civil war in Persia and weakening the Sasanian Empire.

rhahzadh.name: Rhahzadh
rhahzadh.summary: A Sasanian general of Armenian origin, known in Byzantine sources as Rhazates, who served under Shah Khosrow II.

byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628.name: Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628
byzantine-sasanian-war-of-602-628.summary: A 26-year war, the last and most devastating of the Roman–Persian wars, in which Heraclius eventually reversed major Persian gains, but both empires were left exhausted.

byzantine-empire.name: Byzantine Empire
byzantine-empire.summary: The continuation of the Roman Empire centred on Constantinople, which endured through the Middle Ages until the Ottomans took the city in 1453; its people called themselves Romans.

true-cross.name: True Cross
true-cross.summary: In Christian tradition, the original wooden cross on which Jesus was crucified, said to have been recovered in Jerusalem by Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, around 326–328.

house-of-karen.name: House of Karen
house-of-karen.summary: One of the Seven Great Houses of Iran under the Parthian and Sasanian Empires, seated at Nahavand near Ecbatana, holding high administrative rank for centuries.

hephthalites.name: Hephthalites
hephthalites.summary: Central Asian people, also called the White Huns, who built an empire from about 450 CE and were militarily dominant until defeated by Turkic and Sasanian forces in 560.

abd-allah-ibn-amir.name: Abd Allah ibn Amir
abd-allah-ibn-amir.summary: Arab general and governor of Basra under the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates from about 650, who oversaw the pacification of the Sasanian Empire and built up Basra as an administrative hub.

samanid-empire.name: Samanid dynasty
samanid-empire.summary: A Persianate Sunni Muslim dynasty that ruled an empire centered on Khorasan and Transoxiana from 819 to 999, patronizing Persian arts and scholars such as Rudaki and Avicenna.

gorgan.name: Gorgan
gorgan.summary: City in northern Iran near the Caspian Sea, capital of Golestan province, historically also known as Astarabad.

muhammad-ibn-zayd.name: Muhammad ibn Zayd
muhammad-ibn-zayd.summary: Ruler of the Zaydid dynasty of Tabaristan from 884, known as 'the Younger Missionary', whose reign was marked by rebellions and invasions before he died of wounds in 900.

tabaristan.name: Tabaristan
tabaristan.summary: A mountainous region on Iran's Caspian coast, corresponding to today's Mazandaran province, which became the area's common name from the 11th century onward.

g-kt-rks.name: Göktürks
g-kt-rks.summary: A Turkic people of medieval Inner Asia who, under Bumin Qaghan and his sons, overthrew the Rouran Khaganate and founded the First Turkic Khaganate in the 6th century.

kavad-ii.name: Kavad II
kavad-ii.summary: Sasanian King of Kings of Iran briefly in 628, who overthrew and executed his father Khosrow II and made peace with the Byzantines, ending their long war.

hurqus-ibn-zuhayr-as-sa-di.name: Hurqus ibn Zuhayr
hurqus-ibn-zuhayr-as-sa-di.summary: An Arab military commander (d. 658) and founding leader of the Kharijites, who led forces in the conquest of Persia and later fought against Caliph Ali at the Battle of Nahrawan, where he was killed.

hormuzan.name: Hormuzan
hormuzan.summary: Persian aristocrat who governed Khuzestan and fought at the Battle of al-Qādisiyyah; captured by Muslims in 642, he was killed in 644 after being accused of assassinating the caliph Umar.

ahvaz.name: Ahvaz
ahvaz.summary: A city in southwestern Iran on the Karun River, near the Iraqi border, serving as capital of Khuzestan province with a history dating to the Achaemenid period.

jizya.name: Jizya
jizya.summary: Tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Islamic law, historically understood as a fee for protection and exemption from military service.

amr-ibn-al-layth.name: Amr ibn al-Layth
amr-ibn-al-layth.summary: Second ruler of Iran's Saffarid dynasty, reigning from 879 to 901, and younger brother of the dynasty's founder Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar.

balkh.name: Balkh
balkh.summary: A city in northern Afghanistan, historically a center of Zoroastrianism and Buddhism known to Persians as Zariaspa and Greeks as Bactra; capital of ancient Bactria, later devastated by the Mongols.

saffarid-dynasty.name: Saffarid dynasty
saffarid-dynasty.summary: An eastern Iranian dynasty ruling parts of Persia, Khorasan and Makran from 861 to 1002, founded by former coppersmith Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar; among the first native Persian dynasties after the Islamic conquest.

sistan.name: Sistan
sistan.summary: A historical desert region in south-eastern Iran and south-western Afghanistan, bisected by the Helmand River, formerly known as Sakastan, 'the land of the Saka.'

bukhara.name: Bukhara
bukhara.summary: Ancient Silk Road city in what is now Uzbekistan, a major center of Islamic scholarship and birthplace of Imam Bukhari, later capital of the Emirate of Bukhara until 1920.

al-masudi.name: Al-Masudi
al-masudi.summary: A historian, geographer and traveler (c. 896–956), sometimes called the 'Herodotus of the Arabs,' best known for his magnum opus The Meadows of Gold, blending history, geography and biography.

avesta.name: Avesta
avesta.summary: The corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally over centuries before being written down under the Sasanians and later largely lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran.

book-pahlavi.name: Book Pahlavi
book-pahlavi.summary: A cursive script derived from Aramaic during the Sassanid period, used mainly to write Zoroastrian books and documents in Middle Persian.

johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.name: Goethe
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.summary: German polymath (1749–1832) widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language, who also wrote scientific treatises on botany, anatomy and colour and served on the Duke of Weimar's privy council.

muslim-conquest-of-persia.name: Muslim conquest of Persia
muslim-conquest-of-persia.summary: A military campaign in which the Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire between 633 and 651 CE, part of the early Muslim conquests that began under Muhammad in 627/628.

khwaday-namag.name: Khwaday-Namag
khwaday-namag.summary: A lost Middle Persian 'Book of Lords/Kings' from the Sasanian era, recounting Iran's legendary history and believed to be a source for Ferdowsi's later Shahnameh.

vishtaspa.name: Vishtaspa
vishtaspa.summary: Figure in Zoroastrian tradition portrayed as an early follower and royal patron of Zoroaster who helped spread his teachings; traditionally considered a historical king, though obscured by legend.

zoroaster.name: Zoroaster
zoroaster.summary: Iranian religious reformer traditionally dated to the 7th-6th centuries BC (some scholars place him earlier), who became the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism through his hymns, the Gathas.

kayanian-dynasty.name: Kayanian dynasty
kayanian-dynasty.summary: A legendary Iranian dynasty central to the heroic age of the Zoroastrian Avesta and the Shahnameh, Iran's national epic.

abbasid-caliphate.name: Abbasid Caliphate
abbasid-caliphate.summary: The third Islamic caliphate, ruling from 750 to 1258 with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time, known for ushering in the Islamic Golden Age of science and culture.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

transoxiana.name: Transoxiana
transoxiana.summary: A Central Asian region beyond the Amu Darya river, named by Alexander the Great's troops in the 4th century BCE and later a Persian Achaemenid province called Sogdia.

tahirid-dynasty.name: Tahirid dynasty
tahirid-dynasty.summary: A Persian dynasty that governed Khorasan for the Abbasid caliphs from 821 to 873, acting as loyal, largely autonomous viceroys rather than an independent state.

chaturanga.name: Chaturanga
chaturanga.summary: An ancient Indian strategy board game known from around the 7th century CE, considered the common ancestor of chess and related games across Asia.

shatranj.name: Shatranj
shatranj.summary: An old form of chess played in the Sasanian Empire, derived from the Indian game chaturanga, that became the ancestor of modern chess after reaching Europe via Muslim Spain and Sicily.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

zoroastrianism.name: Zoroastrianism
zoroastrianism.summary: An ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of Zoroaster, centred on the deity Ahura Mazda and the choice between truth and chaos, once Greater Iran's dominant faith under the Sassanid Empire.

khosrow-i.name: Khosrow I
khosrow-i.summary: Sasanian King of Kings of Iran from 531 to 579, known as Anushirvan ('the Immortal Soul'), who made peace with the Byzantines in 532, later fought them from 540, sacked Antioch, and captured Dara in 573.

al-fihrist.name: Al-Fihrist
al-fihrist.summary: A tenth-century compendium of Islamic knowledge compiled by Ibn al-Nadim, listing about 10,000 books and thousands of authors, many otherwise lost to history.

ibn-al-nadim.name: Ibn al-Nadim
ibn-al-nadim.summary: A Muslim bibliographer and biographer of Baghdad (c. 932–995) who compiled the encyclopedia Kitab al-Fihrist, a wide-ranging book catalogue.

zend.name: Zend
zend.summary: A Zoroastrian term for Middle Persian translations and commentaries on Avestan scripture, produced in the late Sasanian period for religious instruction of believers who no longer spoke Avestan.

sasanian-empire.name: Sasanian Empire
sasanian-empire.summary: An Iranian empire ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651 AD, founded by Ardashir I to revive the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire; at its height it stretched from Egypt to Central Asia.

academy-of-gondishapur.name: Academy of Gondishapur
academy-of-gondishapur.summary: A Sassanid-era center of learning in Iran with a hospital and library, founded by King Shapur I and considered among history's oldest universities.

umayyad-caliphate.name: Umayyad Caliphate
umayyad-caliphate.summary: Second Islamic caliphate, ruled by the Umayyad dynasty from 661 to 750 from its capital Damascus; expanded Muslim rule across the Maghreb, Iberia, Central Asia and Sindh.

al-khwarizmi.name: Al-Khwarizmi
al-khwarizmi.summary: A mathematician, astronomer and geographer (c. 780-850) of the Islamic Golden Age who worked at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and is regarded as the father of algebra.

gerard-of-cremona.name: Gerard of Cremona
gerard-of-cremona.summary: Italian translator (c. 1114-1187) who rendered Arabic scientific texts, including Ptolemy's Almagest, into Latin while working in Toledo, spreading Greek and Arab knowledge to medieval Europe.

robert-of-chester.name: Robert of Chester
robert-of-chester.summary: 12th-century English Arabist who translated Arabic works into Latin, including al-Khwarizmi's book on algebra in 1145, while working in Iberia.

abd-al-rahman-al-sufi.name: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
abd-al-rahman-al-sufi.summary: A Persian astronomer, living from 903 to 986, who worked at the Buyid court in Isfahan and completed his star catalogue, the Book of Fixed Stars, in 964.

panemone-windmill.name: Panemone windmill
panemone-windmill.summary: A vertical-axis windmill design, the earliest known wind machine, made by the Persians using sail-covered slats around a vertical axle to grind grain or draw water.

ban-m-s-brothers.name: Banū Mūsā brothers
ban-m-s-brothers.summary: Three Persian polymath brothers active in 9th-century Baghdad's House of Wisdom, who translated Greek works and made advances in geometry and astronomy.

book-of-ingenious-devices.name: Book of Ingenious Devices
book-of-ingenious-devices.summary: An illustrated work on mechanical devices and automata published in 850 by the Banū Mūsā brothers at Baghdad's House of Wisdom, describing about one hundred inventions.

al-mansur.name: Al-Mansur
al-mansur.summary: Second Abbasid caliph (714-775) who founded the round city that became the core of Baghdad and is regarded by historians as the true founder of the Abbasid Caliphate.

mu-ammad-ibn-ibr-h-m-al-faz-r.name: Al-Fazari
mu-ammad-ibn-ibr-h-m-al-faz-r.summary: Arab philosopher, mathematician and astronomer who died in 796 or 806.

ya-qub-ibn-tariq.name: Yaqub ibn Tariq
ya-qub-ibn-tariq.summary: Persian astronomer and mathematician who lived in Baghdad and died around 796.

brahmagupta.name: Brahmagupta
brahmagupta.summary: Indian mathematician and astronomer (c. 598–668 CE) credited with formalizing the concept of zero and giving the first clear description of the quadratic formula.

br-hmasphu-asiddh-nta.name: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta
br-hmasphu-asiddh-nta.summary: Main work of the mathematician Brahmagupta, written around 628, containing an early treatment of zero, negative numbers and the quadratic formula, entirely in verse.

rudaki.name: Rudaki
rudaki.summary: A 9th–10th century poet, singer and musician regarded as the first major poet to write in New Persian, who served as a court poet for the Samanids in Bukhara.

avicenna.name: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
avicenna.summary: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in the West as Avicenna, was a leading philosopher and physician of the Islamic Golden Age whose Canon of Medicine remained a standard European medical text until 1650.

adolf-fonahn.name: Adolf Fonahn
adolf-fonahn.summary: Norwegian physician and medical historian (1873–1940) who studied Persian and Arabic medical literature, Tibetan Buddhism, and Leonardo da Vinci's anatomical drawings.

al-kindi.name: Al-Kindi
al-kindi.summary: A Mesopotamian Arab polymath (c. 801-873) hailed as the 'father of Arab philosophy,' who oversaw the translation of Greek texts at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and wrote on subjects from mathematics to medicine.

rashidun-caliphate.name: Rashidun Caliphate
rashidun-caliphate.summary: Early Islamic state (632–661 CE) led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad's death, which rapidly expanded into the dominant power of West Asia and North Africa.

yazdegerd-iii.name: Yazdegerd III
yazdegerd-iii.summary: The last Sasanian King of Kings (632-651), enthroned at age eight, whose defeats by the Rashidun Caliphate ended over four centuries of pre-Islamic Iranian rule; killed near Merv in 651.

merv.name: Merv
merv.summary: A major ancient Iranian city in Central Asia on the Silk Road, settled from the 3rd millennium BC, that at times served as capital of the caliphate and of the Great Seljuk Empire and became a center of Islamic science.

buyid-dynasty.name: Buyid dynasty
buyid-dynasty.summary: A Shia Muslim dynasty of Iranian Daylamite origin that ruled Iraq and central and southern Iran from 934 to 1062, reviving symbols of the Sasanian Empire.

shushtar.name: Shushtar
shushtar.summary: Ancient fortress city in Khuzestan province, Iran, known for an elaborate irrigation system built around the Band-e Kaisar, Iran's first dam bridge.

sabuktigin.name: Sabuktigin
sabuktigin.summary: Founder of the Ghaznavid dynasty who ruled as amir of Ghazna from 977 to 997, a former Turkic slave soldier who expanded his rule into Afghanistan and India.

ghazni.name: Ghazni
ghazni.summary: City in southeastern Afghanistan, historically the capital of the Ghaznavid Empire and today the capital of Ghazni Province.

ghaznavid-empire.name: Ghaznavid Empire
ghaznavid-empire.summary: Persianate Muslim empire of Turkic origin that flourished from 977 to 1186, stretching at its height from the Oxus River to the Indus Valley.

khurramites.name: Khurramites
khurramites.summary: An Iranian religious and political movement rooted in Zoroastrian Mazdakism, also called the Muhammira or 'Red-Wearing Ones' for their symbolic red dress.

sunpadh.name: Sunpadh
sunpadh.summary: An 8th-century Iranian nobleman of the House of Karen who led an uprising against the Abbasid Caliphate.

babak-khorramdin.name: Babak Khorramdin
babak-khorramdin.summary: An Iranian revolutionary leader (795/798–838) who led a rebellion against the Abbasid Caliphate from Azerbaijan, calling for a return of Iran's past political glories.

uthman.name: Uthman ibn Affan
uthman.summary: Third Rashidun caliph (644–656), a companion and son-in-law of Muhammad, best known for standardizing the Quran into the Uthmanic codex.

fars-province.name: Fars province
fars-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran, historically known as Persis, whose capital is the city of Shiraz.

makran.name: Makran
makran.summary: Semi-desert coastal region of Balochistan along the Gulf of Oman, split between Pakistan and Iran.

muhammad-ibn-abi-l-saj.name: Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj
muhammad-ibn-abi-l-saj.summary: Iranian general who founded the Sajid dynasty and governed Azerbaijan from about 889 or 890 until his death in 901.

amu-darya.name: Amu Darya
amu-darya.summary: A major Central Asian river, historically called the Oxus, that flows through Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan and was once seen as the boundary between Greater Iran and Turan.

alid-dynasties-of-northern-iran.name: Alavids
alid-dynasties-of-northern-iran.summary: Zaydi Shia Alid dynasties that ruled Tabaristan in northern Iran between 864 and 928, interrupted briefly by Samanid occupation before being restored.

zaydism.name: Zaydism
zaydism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, also called Fiver Shia, that arose in the eighth century after Zayd ibn Ali's failed rebellion against the Umayyad Caliphate; most followers today live in Yemen.

mazandaran-province.name: Mazandaran
mazandaran-province.summary: An Iranian province on the southern Caspian coast, spanning forests, plains and the Alborz mountains including Mount Damavand, known for agriculture, fish farming and tourism.

daylam.name: Daylaman
daylam.summary: A mountainous inland region of Gilan, Iran, home to the Daylamites and the origin point of the Buyid dynasty around 930.

church-of-the-east.name: Church of the East
church-of-the-east.summary: An Eastern Christian branch, also called the Nestorian Church, that arose from 5th-century Christological disputes and originated in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire.

bactria.name: Bactria
bactria.summary: An ancient Iranian region of Central Asia between the Oxus River and the Hindu Kush, an early centre of Zoroastrianism later ruled by the Achaemenid Empire and conquered by Alexander the Great.

sogdia.name: Sogdia
sogdia.summary: An ancient Iranian civilisation between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, conquered in turn by Persian, Greek and other empires; its merchants were key middlemen on the Silk Road.

muhammad.name: Muhammad
muhammad.summary: The founder of Islam, born around 570 CE in Mecca, whom Muslims believe received revelations from God beginning around 610 as the final prophet.

mazdakism.name: Mazdakism
mazdakism.summary: A Zoroastrian offshoot movement in the Sasanian Empire, founded by Zaradust-e Khuragen and later led by Mazdak, who was executed around 531 by Emperor Khusrau I.

gathas.name: Gathas
gathas.summary: The central hymns of Zoroastrianism, traditionally attributed to Zarathustra and composed in the oldest attested Iranian language, among the oldest surviving Indo-European texts.

asha.name: Asha
asha.summary: A Zoroastrian concept meaning truth, righteousness and cosmic order, central to Zoroastrian theology and personified as the divinity Asha Vahishta.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.summary: The chief god and sky deity of Zoroastrianism, first prominently invoked in the Achaemenid-era Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great.

ahriman.name: Angra Mainyu
ahriman.summary: The destructive evil spirit of Zoroastrianism, the main adversary of the supreme god Ahura Mazda.

achaemenid-empire.name: Achaemenid Empire
achaemenid-empire.summary: Ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, the largest of its time, stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley before Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

dehqan.name: Dehqan
dehqan.summary: A class of land-owning nobles in Iranian lands during the Sasanian and early Islamic periods, who helped preserve Iranian identity and culture until fading away under the Seljuks.

sufism.name: Sufism
sufism.summary: An Islamic spiritual and ethical discipline concerned with purifying the self, closeness to God, and mystical experience, often described as Islamic mysticism.

parsis.name: Parsis
parsis.summary: A Zoroastrian community descended from Persian refugees who fled the Arab-Islamic conquest of Iran in the 7th century, settling mainly in Gujarat and Maharashtra.

bundahishn.name: Bundahishn
bundahishn.summary: Middle Persian text compiling Zoroastrian beliefs about cosmology, mostly dating to the 8th and 9th centuries CE and drawing on the Avesta, though not itself scripture.

persianization.name: Persianization
persianization.summary: The process by which non-Persian peoples and cultures, such as Caucasian and Turkic groups, adopted the Persian language and culture, especially during the early and middle Islamic periods.

persianate-society.name: Persianate
persianate-society.summary: Describes a society shaped by Persian language, literature, art or identity even if not ethnically Persian; examples include the Seljuq, Timurid, Mughal and Ottoman dynasties.
